factor_verdicts.reason: Report shows the established playbook allowed removal of servers supporting subsystems beyond the intended billing-related one, which contributed to the scope of impact.

factors.factor: Command input validation: the capacity-removal command accepted an input that removed a far larger set of servers than intended, and no safeguard caught the mismatch before execution.
factors.evidence: "One of the inputs to the command was entered incorrectly and a larger set of servers was removed than intended."

factors.factor: Tooling and playbook design: the operation was performed using an established playbook that permitted removal of servers supporting multiple subsystems, not only the intended billing-related subsystem.
factors.evidence: "an authorized S3 team member using an established playbook executed a command which was intended to remove a small number of servers for one of the S3 subsystems that is used by the S3 billing process." | "The servers that were removed supported two other S3 subsystems."

factors.factor: Restart and recovery time: restarting the index and placement subsystems and running the metadata integrity safety checks took longer than expected, prolonging the outage.
factors.evidence: "The process of restarting these services and running the necessary safety checks to validate the integrity of the metadata took longer than expected."

factors.factor: Dependency of the health dashboard on the failing service: the Service Health Dashboard admin console depended on S3, so status updates could not be published during the outage.
factors.evidence: "the team was unable to update the individual services' status on the AWS Service Health Dashboard (SHD) because of a dependency the SHD administration console has on Amazon S3."

factors.factor: Cross-service dependency on S3 in the region: many AWS services relying on S3 for storage were impacted when S3 APIs became unavailable.
factors.evidence: "Other AWS services in the US-EAST-1 Region that rely on S3 for storage, including the S3 console, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) new instance launches, Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) volumes (when data was needed from a S3 snapshot), and AWS Lambda were also impacted"

factors.factor: Sequential recovery dependency: the placement subsystem could not recover until the index subsystem was fully functional, serializing recovery and extending the time to full service.
factors.evidence: "The placement subsystem began recovery when the index subsystem was functional and finished recovery at 1:54PM PST."

factors.factor: Backlog accumulation in dependent services: downstream services accumulated work during the outage and needed extra time to recover after S3 was restored.
factors.evidence: "Some of these services had accumulated a backlog of work during the S3 disruption and required additional time to fully recover."

action_items.action: Add input validation and confirmation safeguards to capacity-removal tooling, such as requiring explicit confirmation of the target server count and blocking execution when the count exceeds a defined threshold for the playbook.

Redesign the operational playbook and tooling so that server removal can only target servers serving a single subsystem, and enforce the restriction in code rather than relying on operator input accuracy.
Decouple the index and placement subsystems from the servers used by the billing subsystem so that removing capacity for one subsystem cannot take down others.

Modify the index and placement subsystems to support restart without full-fleet restarts and to complete metadata integrity checks incrementally, and measure restart time against a defined recovery objective.
Remove the Service Health Dashboard admin console's dependency on S3 and host it in a separate failure domain so status updates can be published during an S3 outage.
Create a runbook and automated alerting for communicating status to customers through alternate channels when the primary status dashboard is unavailable.
Map and document regional dependencies on S3 for dependent services such as EC2, EBS, Lambda, and the S3 console, and test degraded-mode behavior for each.

Add a pre-execution check to capacity-removal tooling that calculates the remaining capacity of every subsystem that would be affected and blocks the change if any subsystem would fall below its defined minimum safe threshold; add an alert when live subsystem capacity drops below that threshold. Verify in a test environment that an over-removal attempt is blocked.
Add backpressure and backlog-draining controls to dependent services so they recover in a bounded, predictable time after an upstream outage.
